pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 22: Growing: pea (13 cm). Questions: several.*

The lift was broken again, which was annoying because it had been broken for two hours, but it meant I had to take the stairs. I was on the third landing, counting the grey steps under my trainers, when I heard the scrape of a mop.

Mr. Osei was there, leaning on his handle and staring at a water stain on the floor that looked suspiciously like a map of nowhere. I stopped. I had wanted to ask him about the garden for six days, but every time I opened my mouth, my brain went quiet, which was a new and annoying habit.

"Mr. Osei," I said, and my voice came out thin. I cleared my throat. "Do you know about the garden?"

He did not look up, just kept scrubbing the same circle of concrete.

"There is nothing behind the loading bay," he said, his voice soft like the rustle of dry leaves. "Just a fence."

I waited, but he did not move, and the mop squeaked once, a long, sad sound, before stopping completely.
pages.image: A tall man with a grey moustache and blue overalls mops a circle on a grey concrete stairwell floor, looking down with a calm, distant expression; a girl with round glasses and a denim jacket stands behind him, looking uncertain.

pages.text:
I did not leave. Standing there, I gripped my bag straps until my knuckles went white, while the stairwell air grew thick with the smell of old paint and dampness.

"The bench," I said. "It hums."

Mr. Osei’s hand stopped moving. He looked at me, then down at his keys, the big ring jingling softly against his belt. He stared back at the floor.

"Ada liked that bench," he said.

It was the first time I had heard a name in this building that wasn’t Mrs. Ilves or the mailman. Ada. The name hung in the air, light and fragile. He picked up his bucket. He did not look at me again. He walked past me, his shoes squeaking on the wet patch of floor, and disappeared around the corner.

The lift dinged. It was an awful sound, sharp and brassy. I rode up alone, my face burning. I had asked. I had not answered.
pages.image: A girl with brown skin and round glasses stands alone in a narrow, grey lift, looking down at her hands with a flushed, tense expression; the lift buttons glow faintly in the dim light, and the atmosphere feels heavy and silent.

pages.text:
I took the stairs up from there, mostly because I needed to move my legs and less because I was tired. On the ninety-second step, I found Theo Kowalski.

He was sitting there, legs crossed, wearing a beanie and a hoodie with the sleeves pushed up to his elbows. He was doing nothing, just looking at the wall, and I realized with a shock that this was what he did when he was lonely. He sat on the highest step and watched the concrete.

"You followed me," I said. It wasn't a question.

He shrugged, one shoulder going up. "Yesterday. The fence."

"I said no," I said.

"I know." He picked at a loose thread on his sleeve. "I don't want to tell anyone. I just want to see. And I know about peas."

"Nobody knows about peas," I snapped.

"Grandmother grew forty types," he said, his eyes still on the wall. "In Kraków. On a balcony. She was very strict about the soil."
pages.image: A boy in a beanie and hoodie sits cross-legged on a concrete stair step, looking at the wall with a bored, guarded expression; a girl in a denim jacket stands nearby, arms crossed, looking annoyed but curious.

pages.text:
I stood there. The air in the stairwell felt thick, like the sticky residue left on a spoon after eating cold honey. I thought about the yogurt cup. I thought about the bean I had dug up with the teaspoon. I thought about how I had never let anyone see anything that was mine. Not the list. Not the seed. Not the way my heart beat when I counted steps.

I took a breath. It was a huge breath, the kind that pulls your ribs wide, similar to the gasp before a dive into the school pool in January. The whole body tenses at once. You do not think about the temperature. You just go.

"Yes," I said.

Theo looked at me. He did not smile. He just nodded, once, and stood up. He stretched his back, popping a knuckle with a sound like a dry twig snapping. The concrete under my feet felt solid and real. I felt lighter, and also heavier, as if I had picked up a bag of flour that I would have to carry home.
pages.image: A girl with a green pencil in her hair takes a deep breath, her chest expanding, while a boy in a beanie stands beside her, looking at her with quiet attention; the grey stairwell surrounds them, highlighting the moment of decision.

pages.text:
We went down, out, and through the gap, where the mud was cold and thick on my knees. Theo stopped in the doorway and stood there for a full minute, his hood down and his mouth open. He was looking at the pear tree, the mossy wall, and the rusted tin on the bench.

"It's not a dump," he said, his voice rough. "It's a garden."

The bench hummed, a low, warm sound that vibrated through the wood into the air. It felt like the vibration of a phone on a table, but steady and alive. From under the pear tree, a shadow moved. A mossy shell turned, and a slow, ancient eye blinked.

"Mm," said Gherkin.

He paused. I counted. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten. Eleven.

"Another one," he finished.
pages.image: A boy in a beanie stands in a walled garden doorway, mouth open in awe, looking at a pear tree and a mossy wall; an old tortoise with a mossy shell peers out from under the tree, and a wooden bench sits nearby.
